How to read the atlas

This independent educational atlas follows Swami Vivekananda’s life from 12 January 1863 to 4 July 1902. It gives priority to official Belur Math accounts and the Ramakrishna Order’s publications. Swamiji’s published letters and speeches supply primary evidence for his journeys. Specific official site histories supply details that a brief overview may omit.

It covers the principal documented journeys and selected smaller stops, residences, religious sites and lecture venues. It is not an exhaustive diary of every day or local excursion. A gap on the map means the record has not been reconstructed here.

LabelWhat it means
Exact dateA source supports the calendar day displayed. Age is calculated from 12 January 1863.
Month / year knownThe month or year is supported; no missing day is supplied.
Known period / approximate dateA broad range or narrative sequence is preserved. Timeline placement within a broad period is an editorial ordering aid, not an exact date claim.
Solid connectionThe order of selected stops is documented. The drawn line remains schematic.
Dashed connectionConfirmed places are joined for orientation; their intervening itinerary or precise order has not been fully established.

Every route line is illustrative geometry. No line claims to reproduce an exact road, railway alignment or sea lane. Arrows indicate the displayed direction. Route panels name transport only at the level supported by the evidence. Omitted intermediate stops can make two points appear directly connected.

Markers use present-day geographic coordinates. A temple, monastery or venue is identified where known; otherwise a city or neighbourhood centre is used and labelled in the panel. Countries in the filters refer to present-day geography, including places visited before the partition of British India. Basemap boundaries are contemporary geographic context. India follows the official Indian boundary convention, including the full Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh territories. This is a cartographic convention; territorial claims and administration differ in some border regions. Street-map tiles are provided by CARTO using OpenStreetMap data. The India outline is drawn above those tiles so both the street-map view and the bundled outline map show the same boundary.

Multiple events at one place share a marker and are listed together in the information panel. Filters include an event in any year covered by its displayed range. Approximate ages are conservative ranges based on the known years.

Map boundary sources

India: Survey of India-derived boundary geometry published by the DataMeet India community in its india-soi.geojson dataset. The outline follows the official Indian boundary convention and has been cross-checked against the current Survey of India outline. Source: Survey of India, Government of India; derived data: DataMeet India community.

Other countries: public-domain Natural Earth geometry, distributed by the geo-countries project. Neighbouring polygons are clipped against the displayed India outline to avoid overlapping national outlines. Geometry is generalised for this educational atlas; city and site coordinates are separate from country boundary data.

DataMeet identifies the India geometry as ODbL / CC BY-SA 2.5. The combined and simplified boundary database is made available under ODbL, with attribution to DataMeet and Natural Earth. The historical event dataset is separate.

Official sources take priority

When dates or accounts differ, the atlas follows the relevant official Belur Math account and names it in the event’s source notes. The fuller disciples’ biography and specific histories published by the Order remain important for detail. Where an official source does not establish a day, a month, year or approximate period is retained.

The Order’s official reading portal provides The Life of Swami Vivekananda by His Eastern and Western Disciples and the Complete Works. Chapter citations also link the biography’s transcription hosted by the Order’s university. Supplementary chronologies are used with their own qualifications preserved.

EntryOfficial account followed
Dakshineswar meetingNovember 1881, following Belur Math’s biography. The earlier house encounter remains a separate record.
Shyampukur2 October–11 December 1885, following the specific official site history. These are Sri Ramakrishna’s residence dates, not a claim of Narendra’s continuous attendance.
Belgaum / Belagavi16–27 October 1892, following the official memorial history.
Kanyakumari meditation24–26 December 1892, following the official documentary listing on Belur Math’s website.
Old MathInstitutional use began on 13 February 1898, following the official anniversary site history.
Kakrighat and MeerutKakrighat is dated to 1890. Meerut retains a broad 1890–1891 period because the accounts do not establish exact arrival and departure days.

The timeline, event panels and audio guide use these same decisions. Source review: 3 October 2026. This is an independent educational atlas; use of official historical sources does not imply Belur Math’s endorsement.

Where accounts need care

  • The first meeting with Sri Ramakrishna: the fuller disciples’ biography distinguishes an encounter at Surendra Nath Mitra’s house from the first visit to Dakshineswar. Belur Math’s brief overview compresses the account. The atlas keeps the encounters separate and follows the official November 1881 dating for Dakshineswar. No exact day or interval is asserted.
  • Early travels in Gujarat and southern India: many stops are secure while dates, lengths of stay and some sequences differ. The western tour uses broad ranges. The Madurai, Rameswaram and Kanyakumari visits are not connected as a certain sequence.
  • Kanyakumari: The atlas follows 24–26 December 1892 as published in Belur Math’s official documentary listing. The source is identified as official published dating; the displayed connection does not establish an exact route to the rock.
  • Meerut: the official Akhandananda biography describes months of association with the brother monks, and the fuller biography mentions a roughly five-month stay. A broad period is preserved; precise arrival and departure days are not inferred.
  • Planned pilgrimages: the 1890 attempt to reach Kedarnath and Badrinath was interrupted. Neither is mapped as a completed visit. Plans to travel to Japan in 1902 are likewise not turned into visits.
  • Port calls: a ship’s arrival is not proof of an excursion ashore. In particular, he was prevented from landing at Madras in June 1899.
  • The 1902 Buddha Gaya visit: a biographical reference to his birthday does not by itself establish 12 January, since religious anniversaries also followed the lunar calendar. The visit is displayed by month.
  • Religious experiences: visions, spiritual realisations and Mahasamadhi are represented as reported experiences or the language of the Order’s tradition. An unverified medical diagnosis is not supplied for his death.

The website avoids frequently repeated but unverified travel anecdotes and does not use quotations merely attributed to Swamiji without a traceable text.

Historical references

Each event links to its supporting source and chapter, section or dated entry. Official Belur Math pages are cited first where they resolve an ambiguity; the fuller Order biography supports the more detailed narrative. The Western chronology is a research aid with its own references; its uncertain entries are not promoted to exact dates.

Historical photographs

The images are historical photographs, with captions and attribution. They are not AI illustrations or visual reconstructions. A portrait accompanying the Parliament address is explicitly labelled as a portrait from that period.

About the audio guide

The nine audio chapters are editorial summaries of the same sourced chronology used by the map and timeline. They cover selected highlights rather than every recorded stop. Each transcript passage links to the related event records, where the original historical sources can be opened.

The narrator is Prabhat, a synthesised Indian English voice (en-IN-PrabhatNeural). This is newly produced narration, not a recording of Swami Vivekananda or an imitation of his voice. Spoken paragraph timings connect the audio to confirmed event locations; they do not establish historical dates or exact travel routes.

The spoken guide follows the same official dates as the timeline, including November 1881 at Dakshineswar, 16–27 October 1892 at Belgaum and 24–26 December 1892 at Kanyakumari. It preserves uncertainty about other early travel dates and interrupted pilgrimages. Following the map reveals the narrated stops if your filters hide them. Choosing another event or filter pauses the narration so you can explore at your own pace.

A chronology you can inspect

The event records preserve the displayed date, degree of precision, location, life phase, explanation, significance, uncertainty and sources. Route records separately identify endpoints, stop-order evidence and transport notes. This separation keeps a confirmed visit from becoming an invented route.
